narrative:
The model estimated a 99.2% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is an extremely high risk estimate, and it is the reason your law school application was rejected: the decision treated predicted bar-exam failure as decisive.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this much lower standing pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your first-year class standing, also second decile versus an accepted-student average around the sixth decile, which added another strong push toward failure. Your upper-middle family income bracket was the third most important factor and added a smaller push toward failure; although upper-middle income is common among accepted students, in your case it modestly raised the estimated risk.

To move forward, ask admissions for a formal review or appeal, explaining any circumstances behind your early grades and any upward trend. Meet with a pre-law or bar-readiness advisor to build a concrete plan: strengthen your academic record where possible, prepare for the bar early, and consider retaking the admissions test, since your score is below the accepted average. Then reapply when you can show improved evidence and context, rather than treating this prediction as final.
